pharm: Tricyclic antidepressant that inhibits noradrenaline and serotonin reuptake; activating/antidepressant at low doses and more sedative at higher doses.
quick: Commonly the Deanxit combination (10 mg melitracen/tablet): 2 tablets/day, max 4/day
Take with or without food; dose morning/noon
Not recommended; risk of neonatal withdrawal
Caution; excreted in milk in small amounts
No specific scheme; general TCA caution
Caution in advanced hepatic disease; reduce dose
summary: Melitracen is a tricyclic antidepressant used for depression and anxiety, most commonly marketed as the fixed combination with flupentixol (Deanxit). It inhibits noradrenaline and serotonin reuptake and has a bimodal profile - activating at low doses and sedative at higher doses. It is not FDA-approved or marketed in the US; the data here are drawn from regional SmPC/regulatory sources, predominantly for the combination product. Like other TCAs it has anticholinergic effects and is dangerous in overdose (cardiotoxicity).
indications: Mild to moderate depression with associated anxiety
Depression (as monotherapy in some regional products)

dosage.t: One in the morning and one at noon
dosage.n: Severe cases up to 40 mg (4 tablets)/day; well-documented combination dosing

dosage.t: In the morning (add a noon dose if severe)

dosage.n: Up to ~150-225 mg/day in severe cases per manufacturer summaries; sources conflict

admin: Dose in the morning and at noon to exploit the activating profile and avoid insomnia
Titrate the dose gradually and do not stop abruptly
moa: Melitracen inhibits the presynaptic reuptake of noradrenaline and serotonin (an imipramine analogue) and has histamine H1 affinity contributing to sedation. Its effect is dose-dependent: lower doses are activating and antidepressant, whereas higher doses are more sedative and anxiolytic.

absolute: Concurrent or recent (within 14 days) MAOI therapy
Any degree of heart block, arrhythmia, or coronary insufficiency
Coma or CNS depression (alcohol, barbiturates, opioids)
monitor: ECG in cardiac disease, the elderly, or high doses

preg: Not recommended; discontinue about 14 days before expected delivery because of the risk of neonatal withdrawal and extrapyramidal symptoms. Use only if the benefit clearly outweighs the risk.
lact: Excreted in breast milk in small amounts (comparable to amitriptyline); breastfeeding may be acceptable with observation of the infant.
renal: No specific dose adjustment is defined; observe general tricyclic precautions.
hepatic: Advanced hepatic disease is a precaution - reduce the dose; no quantitative scheme is provided.

major: MAOIs - risk of serotonin syndrome (allow a washout of at least 14 days for irreversible MAOIs)
Sympathomimetics (adrenaline, noradrenaline, ephedrine, phenylephrine) - potentiated pressor effects
moderate: QT-prolonging drugs and antiarrhythmics - arrhythmia risk
minor: Hepatic enzyme inducers/inhibitors - altered TCA levels
interactions.diagnostics: May cause ECG changes; class effect of interfering with catecholamine assays.

rare: Hyperprolactinaemia / sexual dysfunction (mainly the flupentixol component)

monitoring: ECG in patients with cardiac disease, the elderly, or on high doses
Liver function and blood counts on prolonged therapy
counsel: This medicine can either calm or activate you - take it in the morning and at noon, not late at night
Avoid alcohol and take care when driving until you know how it affects you
Report chest pain, palpitations, fainting, severe constipation, urinary retention, or fever with tremor
Do not stop suddenly; tell your doctor if your mood worsens or you have thoughts of self-harm
pk: ~19 to ~62 hours (sources vary; the longer value supports once-daily dosing)
Long; allows once- to twice-daily dosing
Store below 25-30 C, protected from moisture and light
pearls: Not FDA-approved or marketed in the US - data here are from regional SmPC/regulatory sources
Marketed almost exclusively as the Deanxit combination (with flupentixol) for short-term mild depression/anxiety with somatic complaints
Dangerous in overdose (TCA cardiotoxicity) - limit the quantity dispensed in at-risk patients
Long half-life means slow washout when discontinuing or before starting an MAOI
missed: Take the missed dose the same day if remembered; if it is evening or near the next dose, skip it - do not take a double dose.
overdose: Causes anticholinergic toxicity and TCA cardiotoxicity (QRS widening, ventricular arrhythmias, hypotension, seizures, coma). There is no specific antidote. Provide supportive care with continuous ECG monitoring; give IV sodium bicarbonate for QRS widening, arrhythmia, or hypotension; benzodiazepines for seizures; activated charcoal if early and the airway is protected. Avoid Class IA/IC antiarrhythmics.
